item.title: Multifractality of human upper-limb velocity tracks motor optimization via hand dominance experiment
item.description: arXiv:2610.27399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Theoretical goal-directed movements follow a unique, stereotyped velocity profile, but continuous movement has no unique optimal solution, so it is unclear whether motor optimization makes continuous movement more stereotyped or more diverse. Previous studies indicated higher information content in the dominant hand, suggesting greater diversity. Because continuous velocity is a composition of overlapping joints movement of varying form, timing and amplitude, comparable to the events that compose spike trains and heartbeat series, we asked whether this diversity appears as a wider multifractal spectrum of velocity. We applied multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis to motion-capture velocity of cursive handwriting from right- and left-handed participants writing with both hands; hand dominance is a natural experiment in which task and geometry are fixed while optimization varies. With the dominant hand, spectra were wider, had a lower dominant exponent and were more positively asymmetric in both groups, whereas hands with the same functional role did not differ between groups. A logistic regression on the three spectral features identified the dominant hand with a cross-validated AUC of up to 0.93. Optimized continuous movement is thus not more stereotyped but more diverse: complex, neither stereotyped nor random, with multifractality that tracks hand dominance.
item.dc:creator: Yago Emanoel Ramos, Jos\'e Garcia Vivas Miranda

item.title: Does a Flux-Defined Markov Blanket Screen Self-Replicating Gray--Scott Spots? A Computational Test of a Blanket Condition from the Free Energy Principle
item.description: arXiv:2610.27235v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Friston's free energy principle holds that a system separated from its environment by a Markov blanket---a boundary whose states statistically screen its interior from its exterior---can be treated as performing approximate Bayesian inference, and that such blankets arise wherever coupling is short-range. We test this blanket condition in a concrete nonlinear pattern-forming system: self-replicating spots in a reaction-diffusion model that persist, compete, and reproduce. Directed boundary exchange and timescale separation hold up reasonably well, with qualifications. A flux-defined blanket does not screen interior from exterior. Flux removes only part of the linear dependence, and a nonlinear test shows that conditioning on flux \emph{increases} the dependence, consistent with conditioning on a collider, since flux is a joint function of concentrations on both sides of the boundary. The dependence is concentrated within about one organism radius of the boundary. A band of the surrounding field that thick screens the interior from the exterior beyond it, as any short-range field would, which is not evidence of inference.
item.dc:creator: John E Pearson

item.title: Predator-Prey Model: Driven Hunt for Accelerated Grokking
item.description: arXiv:2509.10562v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A machine learning method is proposed using two agents (representing two coupled replicas of the model parameters) that simulate the biological behavior of a predator and a prey. In this method, the two agents interact with each other via a pair of potentials that simulate the dynamics when the predator chases the prey while the prey runs away from the predator - to perform an optimization on the landscape. This method allows, for optimization landscapes with narrow ravines with gentle slope or even flat bottoms, to avoid optimization getting stuck in a ravine. For some examples of grokking (i.e., delayed generalization) problems we show that this method allows for achieving up to a hundred times faster learning in gradient evaluations and up to 60 times in the wall-clock time compared to the standard learning procedure.
item.dc:creator: I. A. Lopatin, S. V. Kozyrev, A. N. Pechen

item.title: Ising-machine-like Driving Condition Restrictions in SSBM and Additional Pseudo-annealing- Driving Method for SSBM that Achieves Best Cut Value Search -
item.description: arXiv:2608.12545v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In our previous work, we proposed and experimentally demonstrated a physics-based simulator for combinatorial optimization problems (SSBM), which exploits a distinctive spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) phenomenon identified in a dissipative system exhibiting robust causality described by an iterative equation. We further conducted numerical simulations in which initial fluctuations of distinct patterns were applied to large-scale benchmark problems, and reported that the SSBM exhibits a unique behavior absent in conventional Ising machines: under specific conditions, pseudo-spin patterns progressively converge during the solution-search process and ultimately coalesce into a single pattern, with the cut value of the converged solution reaching 99.7% of the best-known cut value. In the present paper, we elucidate the conditions under which the SSBM can be configured to emulate the behavior of a continuous-variable Ising machine. We further demonstrate that by additionally incorporating an effect analogous to physical annealing into these conditions, the SSBM becomes capable of identifying the best-known cut value for the K_2000 benchmark instance.
item.dc:creator: Toshiya Sato
